title: Tech CEOs have pivoted from doom to reassurance before
excerpt: Each new wave of technology has sparked job-loss fears for different reasons. The initial shock wears off over time as jobs return in new forms
content_html:
Anthony Lopopolo

Fri, August 14, 2026 at 3:47 PM EDT 7 min read

AI executives who months ago warned that their own technology would displace millions of workers are now walking those predictions back. The reversal happened in under a year. Dire forecasts of mass unemployment gave way to reassurance about augmentation, retraining, and new categories of work.

The speed of the pivot feels unprecedented, but the playbook behind it is nearly a century old. Every major technology wave since electrification — from factory automation in the 1960s to the early internet and offshoring of the 2000s — produced the same cycle of alarm and retreat. Industry leaders amplified displacement fears, public backlash threatened adoption, and leaders reversed course with organized reassurance.

New jobs materialized, and economies adapted. But the transition played out over decades. Jobs came back in different forms, and economic gains flowed to shareholders and higher-skilled workers while the displaced waited for retraining programs that never quite kept pace.

The electrification script and its organized backlash

In 1929, at the peak of a decade-long industrial boom, a committee chaired by Herbert Hoover published a landmark report through the National Bureau of Economic Research that named the problem "technological unemployment." The Report of the Committee on Recent Economic Changes acknowledged that electrification and mechanization were displacing factory workers but offered reassurance, noting that newly expanded service industries had absorbed the displaced and that "the acceleration of technological shifts in production and consumption would have resulted in much more serious unemployment if workers had not been absorbed in the newly expanded service industries."

Then the Depression hit, driving unemployment to historic levels. All the while, the machines kept running. By 1937, factories had almost matched their 1929 output, but with a smaller workforce. Some 20% more jobs would've been needed just to return unemployment to pre-crash levels, according to studies economic historian Amy Sue Bix surveyed in "Inventing Ourselves Out of Jobs?"

The business community's response, as Bix documented, was to mount an organized defense of mechanization. The 1933 Century of Progress exhibition in Chicago and the 1939 World of Tomorrow exhibition in New York sold millions of visitors on the promise of new machines and cheaper goods. The argument was simple: America would invent its way out of the crisis.

Online commerce and the disappearing middleman

Neither side won the argument. According to economic historian Gregory R. Woirol, the electrification-era debate simply faded as World War II sent millions into the military and millions more into arms factories. It happened again in the 1960s, when fears about automation prompted President Lyndon B. Johnson to create a Blue-Ribbon National Commission on Technology, Automation, and Economic Progress. The commission concluded that "technology eliminates jobs, not work." But it was the Vietnam War, not the commission's findings, that ended the anxiety. Wartime spending and conscription soaked up workers faster than any machine could replace them.

2026 年 8 月 14 日星期五，美国东部时间下午 3:47 阅读 7 分钟

人工智能高管几个月前警告称，他们自己的技术将取代数百万工人，但现在却收回了这些预测。 逆转发生在不到一年的时间里。 对大规模失业的可怕预测让位于对增加、再培训和新工作类别的保证。

转型的速度让人感觉前所未有，但其背后的策略已有近一个世纪的历史。 自电气化以来的每一次重大技术浪潮——从 20 世纪 60 年代的工厂自动化到 2000 年代的早期互联网和离岸外包——都产生了同样的警报和撤退周期。 行业领导者加剧了人们对流离失所的担忧，公众的强烈反对威胁了采用，而领导者则通过有组织的保证改变了方向。

新的就业机会出现，经济也随之适应。 但这种转变持续了数十年。 就业机会以不同的形式回归，经济收益流向股东和高技能工人，而失业者则等待着从未跟上步伐的再培训计划。

电气化脚本及其有组织的反弹

1929 年，在长达十年的工业繁荣顶峰时期，由赫伯特·胡佛 (Herbert Hoover) 领导的委员会通过国家经济研究局发布了一份具有里程碑意义的报告，将这一问题命名为“技术失业”。 近期经济变化委员会的报告承认电气化和机械化正在取代工厂工人，但也提供了保证，指出新扩张的服务业已经吸纳了失业者，并且“如果工人没有被新扩张的服务业吸收，生产和消费技术转变的加速将导致更严重的失业”。

随后大萧条来袭，失业率升至历史最高水平。 整个过程中，机器一直在运转。 到 1937 年，工厂的产量几乎与 1929 年持平，但劳动力较少。 经济历史学家艾米·苏·比克斯 (Amy Sue Bix) 在《发明我们自己失业？》一书中进行的调查显示，为了使失业率恢复到崩溃前的水平，就需要增加约 20% 的就业机会。

正如 Bix 所记录的那样，商界的反应是对机械化进行有组织的防御。 1933 年芝加哥的“进步世纪”展览和 1939 年纽约的“明日世界”展览凭借新机器和更便宜的商品吸引了数百万参观者。 论点很简单：美国将发明摆脱危机的方法。

在线商务和消失的中间商

这场争论双方都没有获胜。 根据经济历史学家 Gregory R. 在沃罗尔看来，随着第二次世界大战让数百万人参军，还有数百万人进入军火工厂，有关电气化时代的争论就逐渐消失了。 这种情况在 20 世纪 60 年代再次发生，当时对自动化的担忧促使美国总统林登·B·肯尼迪 (Lyndon B. 约翰逊将创建一个蓝带国家技术、自动化和经济进步委员会。 该委员会的结论是“技术消除了工作岗位，而不是工作”。 但结束焦虑的是越南战争，而不是委员会的调查结果。 战时开支和征兵对工人的吸收速度比任何机器都可以取代他们更快。
